review.title: Provider outbound HTTP resolves, classifies and pins its destination
review.acceptance: THE CANONICAL HOST AND NETWORK POLICY MOVES TO A DEPENDENCY-LEAF PACKAGE, @liberty/net-policy, and both existing classifiers consume it. This replaces the original design, which was 'provider-sdk adopts media-inspection's resolve-and-pin control'; that is preserved in acceptanceOriginal and is NOT to be implemented. WHY THE DESIGN CHANGED, because the reason is the whole point: PL-0709 had to import provider-sdk's classifyHost from media-inspection BY DEEP RELATIVE PATH to write its agreement test, since classifyHost is not exported from packages/provider-sdk/src/index.ts and that package's exports field is a bare ./src/index.ts with no subpaths. The reviewer accepted that import FOR THAT TEST ONLY AT THAT TREE and ruled it is not an acceptable permanent boundary. Making media-inspection depend on provider-sdk, or provider-sdk on media-inspection while media-inspection imports provider-sdk to compare, CREATES OR INVITES A WORKSPACE DEPENDENCY CYCLE -- PL-0710 has provider-sdk adopting media-inspection's authoriseFetchTarget, so the arrow already points the other way. A lower shared layer with NO dependency on provider-sdk or media-inspection is the shape that works. REQUIRED, extraction half: the canonical host and IP classification vocabulary and its normalisation move into @liberty/net-policy; provider-sdk consumes that shared classifier; media-inspection consumes that shared classifier; PL-0709's deep cross-package test import is REMOVED; and the agreement test becomes unnecessary as two implementations become one -- replace it with tests of the shared classifier PLUS package-boundary tests proving both consumers actually import it, because an extraction nothing imports is a third copy rather than a merge. The package name may follow repository convention, but the package must be a dependency leaf. REQUIRED, resolve-and-pin half, unchanged from the original and each clause a separate way host-literal checking fails: DNS resolution before the outbound connection; EVERY resolved address classified, not just the first; refusal if ANY resolved address is private, loopback, link-local or reserved, unless an explicitly permitted local-only path applies; the connection PINNED to the approved resolved address so DNS rebinding cannot change the destination between check and connect; resolution, classification and pinning repeated PER REDIRECT HOP; and TLS CERTIFICATE HOSTNAME VERIFICATION AND SNI REMAIN AGAINST THE ORIGINAL HOSTNAME, NOT THE PINNED IP -- pinning the transport must not turn into verifying the wrong name. Regressions required for public-name-to-private-IP, DNS rebinding, mixed public and private answer sets, and translated-address cases. ALSO IN SCOPE BECAUSE THE EXTRACTION PUTS IT IN PLAY: pin.ts's normaliseHost does not fold the DNS root label. It is safe today because both sides of that comparison come from the same URL object so they carry or omit the dot together, and a mismatch refuses the connection -- but it is a third canonicaliser, and this is the task that removes the others. WHY THIS IS P0: F1, F7 and F8 were three host spellings in one function, and F12 was a fourth spelling in a SECOND function written specifically to avoid duplicating the first. The duplication got in anyway -- not as a copied classifier but as a copied assumption about what a hostname string is. A check comparing a string against literals is only ever as complete as the list of spellings whoever wrote it thought of; resolve-and-pin classifies the address a resolver returned, which has one spelling. FOLDED IN 2026-09-20 from the PL-0305 handoff's remaining off-surface item, because this task already owns both packages and the packaging metadata: @liberty/media-inspection's exports field has no ./http subpath, so importing @liberty/catalog-ingestion from apps/web pulls hls.ts into the program and needs an ambient m3u8-parser shim reached by a triple-slash reference in the ingestion package's index. That reference is the smallest honest fix from inside that package and is not the fix. THE SAME DEFECT SHAPE AS THE ONE THIS TASK EXISTS FOR: provider-sdk's classifyHost is unreachable from outside its package for exactly the same reason, a bare ./src/index.ts exports field with no subpaths, which is why PL-0709 had to import it by deep relative path. Give @liberty/media-inspection the subpath exports its consumers actually need and remove the triple-slash workaround, and make sure @liberty/net-policy is published with the subpaths ITS two consumers need rather than repeating the omission in the new package.

review.title: An agent instruction file has provenance, or it is not an instruction
review.acceptance: Repository validation detects any AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md under a working directory that is not on an explicit, reviewed allowlist, and the authoritative instruction hierarchy is stated somewhere an agent reads before it starts. THE CONCRETE CASE: apps/web/AGENTS.md is GENERATED BY next dev and instructs agents to read node_modules/next/dist/docs/ before writing code. Nothing acted on it, and it is almost certainly benign. The finding is not that file -- it is that framework tooling can write an instruction file into a directory agents treat as authoritative, which makes a dependency's postinstall a path into the control plane's instruction surface. Required: the allowlist names each legitimate instruction file and who owns it, so an unowned one is a validation failure rather than a judgement call; generated instruction files are either gitignored and removed or allowlisted after being read, and the choice is recorded per file; validation fails on an unexpected file rather than warning, because a warning in a passing run is not a control; a regression plants an unexpected AGENTS.md and observes the failure, since a detector nobody has seen fire is not known to work; and the instruction hierarchy is written down -- which file wins, and that nothing under node_modules is ever authoritative. WHAT THIS TASK MUST NOT DO: silently delete a file a framework needs, or treat allowlisting as review. An allowlisted generated file must have been READ by a human or an agent that reports what it says.

review.title: A property suite gets a timeout of its own, not vitest's default
review.acceptance: packages/contracts declares its own vitest testTimeout, with the reason for the value written down, so its fast-check property suite is not running against a default it can exhaust under load. THIS CLOSES AN OPEN ITEM RATHER THAN OPENING ONE. Round 52 recorded a single observed-but-unreproduced failure in stream-candidate.property.test.ts and the lead could not reproduce it across ten seeds; the PL-0710 part-A work reproduced it deterministically and it was never seed-dependent. It is CONCURRENCY-dependent: the box has 2 cores, turbo's default concurrency is 10, the new @liberty/net-policy package takes the graph from 18 test tasks to 20, and 'refuses a licence endpoint that is not https, whatever else it is' -- which runs in 1.73s standalone -- measured 5.4s and 7.4s under that graph against vitest's 5000ms default. Characterised rather than re-rolled: the same tree at --concurrency=4 passes, and the same tree filtered to 19 tasks at default concurrency passes. Required: the timeout is justified against the suite's measured standalone cost and the headroom a loaded machine needs, not picked round; the config explains that a property suite's cost is a function of run count and machine load rather than of the code under test, so a default sized for unit tests is the wrong instrument; and NOTHING ABOUT THE PROPERTY ITSELF IS WEAKENED -- not the run count, not the generators, not an assertion. Raising a timeout to hide a genuinely slow property would be the same mistake one level out, so if the suite is slow for a reason the code should answer for, say so instead. Out of scope: a turbo concurrency cap, which is a CLI flag rather than a turbo.json key and is a CI decision.

I THEN RAN THE RED DIRECTION MYSELF AND IT DID NOT REPRODUCE: with this file removed, the same command on the same tree exited 0. It is headroom for a suite measured to be running at roughly a third of the budget it was held to, with no margin, which is a latent fragility whether or not it fires on a given afternoon. Round 52's single unexplained failure in this same suite is BEST EXPLAINED by this and is not thereby proven to be it; that item stays open rather than being closed on a hypothesis. recommended.title: Contract module boundaries
recommended.acceptance: Shared vocabularies live in their own leaf modules, domain contracts live in one module each, index.ts is a re-export-only compatibility barrel rather than the authoritative public surface, and a wildcard exports map lets a new domain contract be added without touching package metadata or the barrel; no cycle-driven z.lazy remains and structural regressions prove the boundary rather than merely reflecting it; no schema behaviour changes

recommended.title: Profile model
recommended.acceptance: Profiles are modelled above authentication rather than inside the auth library, with the active profile carried alongside the session rather than inside the identity record; profile scoping is present in the first migration rather than retrofitted, because that is the part that is expensive to reverse; profiles can be created and selected with authorization tests

recommended.title: Provider health contract
recommended.acceptance: A provider with zero observations reports unknown with a null observed success rate and a zero sample count, never a mid-range score and never a pass; any prior used to rank an unobserved provider is labelled as a prior rather than presented as measured availability; degraded-but-usable is a state distinct from up and down; health output is pure over the observations plus an explicit policy version, with no hidden wall-clock decay; and health never affects entitlement, so a provider at perfect health still cannot make an unauthorized candidate eligible

typecheck.evidence: turbo run typecheck --filter @liberty/provider-sdk exit 0 under pinned Node 22 resolved via npx node@22.

unit.evidence: turbo run test --filter @liberty/provider-sdk exit 0 under pinned Node 22: zero observations yielding unknown with a null observed rate and a zero sample count, a prior labelled rather than presented as measurement at the same ranking number as a measured value, the degraded band held distinct from up and down, purity over observations plus an explicit policy version with Date.now replaced by a thrower to prove no wall clock is read, whole-report permutation invariance under generated policies, monotonicity in each count, and a compile-time guard that no health type can carry entitlement.

recommended.title: Production composition registers the catalog ingestion runtime
recommended.acceptance: A hosted deployment that is configured for a real catalog source actually gets one: something in the production composition root calls registerCatalogIngestionRuntime with a runtime built next to the Node pinned-fetch construction. PL-0305 made the application CAPABLE of hosting the real source and the reviewer accepted that as complete; what remains is that NOTHING CALLS THE REGISTRATION, so a hosted deployment still answers no_metadata_source_configured -- a true statement about the deployment rather than about the registry, and the exact gap this task owns. Required: the runtime is built from the existing pinned-fetch transport rather than a second fetch path; NO CREDENTIAL OR API KEY IS INTRODUCED, since the initial source needs none and an ambient key would be the hidden credentialed source PL-0305's review forbade; an unconfigured deployment must STILL refuse by name rather than silently acquiring a default; and a regression must drive the composition root and observe a configured resolution, because a registration nobody has watched fire is not known to work. OUT OF SCOPE: persistent scheduling and storage, which is PL-0309, and the rights register, which is not a coding task. NOTE BEFORE CLAIMING: the exact composition-root file may not exist yet; the declared surface names the likely homes and must be corrected before the claim rather than widened after, on the PL-0710 precedent.

recommended.title: release clears the implementation base, or a re-claim inherits a stale one
recommended.acceptance: ai:release clears implementationBaseSha, so a task returned to an unowned queue and later re-claimed records the base of the round that actually implements it. OBSERVED, not hypothesised: PL-0710 was claimed and started at 33195d593695618b779ab6c97a50817a2694e8df, released with nothing written when its implementing agent was terminated, and re-claimed at HEAD 20edec3aa3f33dbd58aa405d1210f56ce54c207f -- and start reported 'started from 33195d593695', preserving the stale base rather than capturing HEAD. CLAUDE.md says implementationBaseSha is the exact lower bound of the first review range and that the range validator refuses a base that is either wider or narrower, so a preserved base makes the published window wider than the implementation. The rule release already follows is the argument: it discards gate results because 'evidence belongs to one implementation round under one owner', and a base is evidence of where that round began. Required: release clears the base, and ai:unblock is checked for the same defect and fixed if it has it; a scenario in scripts/test-ai-control-plane.mjs claims, releases, re-claims at a different HEAD and asserts the second base is the second HEAD, because this defect is invisible until exactly that sequence occurs; and the fix must NOT let start overwrite a base on an ordinary re-start of a task that was never released, since that is the falsification --reconcile-existing exists to prevent. Do NOT hand-edit any existing task's recorded base as part of this work; PL-0703 was blocked for that move and the historical records stay as they are.
